what_its_for: Butorphanol is a strong pain reliever (opioid) used to treat moderate to severe pain, such as pain after surgery or injury. It is also sometimes used to treat migraine headaches and as part of anesthesia care.
how_to_take: Butorphanol nasal spray is sprayed into one nostril as directed by your doctor. Tilt your head slightly forward, insert the tip of the spray into one nostril, and press the pump firmly once while breathing in gently through your nose. Do not blow your nose right after using it. If a second dose is needed, spray into the OTHER nostril. Always follow your doctor's exact instructions on how many sprays to use and how often.
dosing: The usual adult dose for the nasal spray is 1 spray (1 mg) in one nostril. Your doctor may tell you to repeat this dose in the other nostril after 60 to 90 minutes if your pain is not relieved. Do NOT use more than your doctor prescribed. Doses are spaced at least 3 to 4 hours apart. Your doctor will decide the right dose for you based on your pain level and medical history.
missed_dose: Butorphanol is usually taken only when you have pain, not on a regular schedule. If your doctor has put you on a specific dosing schedule and you miss a dose, take it as soon as you remember — but ONLY if you are still in pain. If it is almost time for your next dose, skip the missed dose and continue with your regular schedule. Never take two doses at the same time to make up for a missed one.
storage: Store butorphanol nasal spray at room temperature, between 59°F and 86°F (15°C to 30°C). Keep it away from heat, direct light, and freezing temperatures. Keep the cap on the bottle when not in use. Keep this medicine out of the reach of children and pets. Do not flush unused medicine down the toilet — ask your pharmacist about a drug take-back program or proper disposal instructions.
what_to_avoid: Avoid drinking alcohol while using butorphanol — this can cause dangerous drowsiness, slow breathing, or even death. Do not drive, operate heavy machinery, or do any activity that requires you to be fully alert until you know how this medicine affects you. Avoid taking sleeping pills, anti-anxiety medicines, muscle relaxers, or other opioid pain medicines without your doctor's knowledge. Do not use this medicine more often or in larger amounts than prescribed.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor right away or go to the emergency room if you experience: very slow, shallow, or stopped breathing; extreme drowsiness or difficulty waking up; confusion or unusual behavior; dizziness or fainting; a fast or irregular heartbeat; severe nausea or vomiting; signs of an allergic reaction such as rash, swelling of the face or throat, or difficulty breathing. Also contact your doctor if your pain is not being controlled or if you feel you are becoming dependent on the medication.
when_it_works: Butorphanol nasal spray usually starts working within 15 minutes of use. You should feel meaningful pain relief within 30 to 60 minutes. The pain-relieving effects typically last about 4 to 6 hours. If you do not notice any relief after the first dose and the second optional dose, contact your doctor rather than taking extra doses on your own.
special_populations: ELDERLY: Older adults are more sensitive to the effects of butorphanol and may be at higher risk for dizziness, falls, confusion, and breathing problems. Doctors often start with a lower dose. PREGNANCY: Butorphanol can cause serious breathing problems in a newborn if used near the time of delivery. Do not use this medicine during pregnancy unless your doctor has carefully weighed the risks and benefits. Prolonged use can cause dependence in the unborn baby. BREASTFEEDING: Butorphanol passes into breast milk. Talk to your doctor before breastfeeding while using this medicine. LIVER OR KIDNEY DISEASE: If you have liver or kidney problems, your body may process this medicine more slowly, increasing the risk of side effects. Your doctor may prescribe a lower dose or longer intervals between doses. CHILDREN: The safety and effectiveness of butorphanol in children under 18 years of age have not been established; it is generally not recommended for use in children.
